segments.text: Now the part that matters, because you don't choose who you love based on a number, but you do choose who you borrow from, who you sit next to, who you split a bill with. And all of that was being decided quietly by a calculation nobody ever said out loud.

Now it's said out loud constantly. The dinner bill stops being a negotiation and becomes an arithmetic problem. Somebody earns four times what somebody else earns, and everyone at the table can see it, and there is no version of, "Let's just split it," that isn't now a statement. So the split stops being generous and starts being accurate, which sounds fair and feels like being weighed. Then the sorting happens, and it happens faster than anyone expected. Not by class, by number. People with similar numbers start spending time together, not out of snobbery, but because it's the only way a social life stops being a negotiation. If you can see everyone's number, the least awkward thing to do is stand near people who are roughly where you are. Within a month, you could walk into any room and see that it was sorted, not by who they were, by what they had. And here's the thing that should bother you more than it does. That sorting was already happening. We were already doing it with postcodes, with schools, with which restaurant we suggested, with which party we didn't invite someone to. The number didn't create the sorting, it just stopped us being able to pretend it was about something else.

Now the version of this that nobody is ready for, family. You can see your parents' number all the time, falling slowly and then not slowly, and they can see yours. There's a conversation every family eventually has about money, who is helping whom, what's fair, what's owed. It's usually had late and badly and with a great deal left unsaid. With the number public, that conversation is never had at all because the information is already there and nobody has to be the one to bring it up, which sounds like it spares you the awkwardness. What it actually removes is the moment when someone decides to tell you. That moment, the one where your father chooses to be honest with you, is not a transaction. It is the relationship. The number gives you the data and takes away the conversation. And over time, you will find that you would rather have had the conversation.
